The Story of Sudarshan

I bow to the Lord Arhants, Siddhas, Acharyas, Upadhyays, and Sadhus — the five supreme beings who bestow the bliss of liberation — and I write the story of Sudarshan, who attained liberation through the worship of the Panch Namaskar Mantra.

In the city of Champa, capital of Angadesh, there ruled a king named Gajvahan. He was handsome and a mighty warrior, and by his valour he had conquered all enemies and made his kingdom free from trouble. In the same city lived a merchant named Vrishabhdatt, whose wife was Arhaddasi. The merchant loved his wife dearly, and she was a devoted and virtuous wife, ever absorbed in devotion to Lord Jina.

Vrishabhdatt employed a cowherd as a servant. One winter evening, as the cowherd was returning home from the forest, he saw an ascetic endowed with supernatural powers, seated in meditation upon a rock. Seeing the monk, the cowherd was moved to pity, thinking, "Alas! He has no clothing, and the cold is fierce, yet he will spend the night sitting on this very rock." He went home, and at midnight returned with his wife to the monk. The sage was still seated in meditation, just as he had been. His entire body was drenched with dew. Moved by compassion, the cowherd wiped the dew from the monk's body and spent the whole night pressing his feet and serving him in every way he could.

At dawn the monk completed his meditation. Opening his eyes, he found the cowherd sitting nearby. Recognizing him as a soul near to liberation, the monk taught him the Panch Namaskar Mantra, which is the cause of attaining heaven and liberation. Then, chanting the mantra himself, the monk departed through the sky.

Gradually the cowherd developed great faith in the mantra. Before beginning any task, he would first recite the Namaskar Mantra. One day, as the cowherd was chanting the mantra, his master overheard him and asked with a smile, "Where did you pick up this mantra?" The cowherd told his master the whole story. The merchant was pleased and said, "Brother, what does it matter that you were born in a humble family? Your devotion has made you worthy of this sacred knowledge." The merchant himself began practising the mantra with great devotion.

Through constant recitation and meditation upon the Namaskar Mantra, both the cowherd and the merchant purified their souls. The cowherd, whose name was Sudarshan, attained such spiritual heights that he eventually renounced the world, became a monk, and through deep meditation on the five supreme beings, destroyed all his karmas and attained liberation — the eternal, blissful state of the Siddhas.

This story teaches that the Panch Namaskar Mantra is a supreme spiritual practice accessible to all, regardless of birth or station. Even a humble cowherd, through sincere devotion to this mantra, attained the highest goal of human life. The mantra needs no elaborate ritual — only a pure heart and steadfast faith.
